The era in north India, roughly 1500 to 600 BCE, when the Vedas were composed. It falls between the end of the Indus cities and the rise of new cities and kingdoms along the Ganges. Its dates are inferred mostly from the language of the texts, not from archaeology.

The Vedas are hymns and ritual texts in Vedic Sanskrit, an early Indo-Aryan language brought into the subcontinent by the Indo-Aryan migrations. They were handed down by memory for many centuries before being written. Much of what we know about the period comes from them.

Two phases are usually seen:

  • Early Vedic (about 1500 to 1100 BCE). The Rigveda was composed in the Punjab. Its people were herders who prized cattle and horses, raced chariots, and lived in tribes led by chiefs. They worshipped gods such as Indra and Agni with fire sacrifices.
  • Later Vedic (about 1100 to 600 BCE). People moved east into the Ganges plain, cleared forest with iron tools and grew rice. Tribes merged into kingdoms such as the Kuru and Panchala. The other Vedas, the ritual handbooks and the first Upanishads were composed. The four-part social order of the varnas hardened.

Archaeologists link the later phase with the Painted Grey Ware culture. The era gave Indian civilisation its sacred language, many of its rituals and ideas of karma and rebirth. It ended as the Mahajanapadas rose and teachers like the Buddha and Mahavira challenged Vedic sacrifice.
